tour.title: Temple City: Chikhan Tower, Confucius & Shennong Street
tour.summary: A Ming prince's grave, the island's first school, a war god and a sea goddess, a Dutch fort, a river-port lane and the best food street in Taiwan — four flat kilometres through the old capital.
tour.overviewText:
Tainan is where Taiwan began: the island's oldest city, its capital for two centuries, and a place that still behaves like the centre of things. January is the best weather the island gets — mild, dry, clear-skied, the crush of summer humidity still months away — which makes this the season to walk it slowly, the only speed at which the route works.

The place. Taiwan's official name is the Republic of China; Beijing claims the island as a province of the People's Republic of China, and most residents favour the current, ambiguous status quo. Tainan is older than that argument. In 1624 the Dutch East India Company — a Dutch trading firm with its own warships — put a base on a sandbar here and called it Tayouan, the name most scholars think became "Taiwan". They built two forts, Zeelandia on the coast and Provintia inland in 1653, to corner the trade in silk, sugar, porcelain and deer skins. In 1661 a Ming loyalist warlord, Zheng Chenggong — better known as Koxinga — took Provintia and, after a nine-month siege, expelled the Dutch, making this the capital of his Kingdom of Tungning. The Qing empire absorbed the island in 1683 and ruled from these streets until 1887, when the capital moved north. The city's name means "south of Taiwan".

Religion is the city's second language. Tainan has more temples per square kilometre than anywhere in Taiwan, and almost all of them are folk temples rather than purely Buddhist or Daoist ones. You will meet Mazu, the sea goddess — a real Fujian woman, Lin Moniang, who was deified; Guan Gong, a third-century general turned god of loyalty and war; city gods who judge the dead; Wenchang, who helps students pass exams; and Yue Lao, who ties couples together with a red thread. People move between Buddhist, Daoist and local belief without noticing the joins: flip two crescent wooden blocks called jiaobei on a temple floor and you have posed a yes-or-no question and been answered. One stop sits apart from all this — the Confucius Temple — because Confucius was a teacher, not a god, and his temple honours the scholarly tradition and the exam system it fed.

Tainan is also, by local consensus, the best place to eat in Taiwan: beef soup for breakfast, danzi noodles, milkfish from the coastal ponds, and sugar in almost everything. Expect a city that discusses lunch the way other cities discuss football.

The walk runs about four kilometres through the old core: graves and academies in the south, north to the temple cluster and Dutch fort at Chihkan, then west down the old river-port lane of Shennong Street to the food street, Guohua. Give it half a day, with pauses for tea.

Almost all of it is free: the temples ask nothing, and only Chihkan Tower (around NT$70) and the inner sanctuary of the Confucius Temple (about NT$50) charge. NT$ is the New Taiwan dollar, the local currency — carry small notes, because food stands mostly take cash. Temples open early, around 06:00, and close between 17:00 and 21:30; confirm hours and fees at each gate, because they move.

Start where the story starts, at a Ming prince's grave, and end where the city lives: at a table. Then eat.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Almost entirely flat city pavements and lanes, with a few raised temple thresholds to step over and one long-ish crossing of the old town. Roughly four kilometres, walked as a half-day with long pauses. The Chihkan Tower pavilions have steps and a steep upper stair; the tomb-shrine and the Confucius Temple grounds are level.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 09:30 or 10:00. The Five Concubines temple gates open at 08:00 and most temples are open by then; the Confucius Temple closes at 17:30, so it has to come before the day runs out, while Chihkan Tower stays open late. Finishing on Guohua Street at lunch or dinner is ideal. January is Tainan's dry, mild season, and weekdays are calmer than weekends.

stops.name: Temple of the Five Concubines
stops.narration:
This quiet walled garden is a tomb with a temple in front of it, and it explains how a dynasty ended here. In 1683 the Qing empire — ruled by the Manchus, a people from China's north-east who had taken the Ming throne in 1644 — sent the admiral Shi Lang to seize this island from the Zheng family, the Ming loyalists who had ruled it since Koxinga expelled the Dutch in 1662.

When the news reached Tainan, one Ming prince in the city, Zhu Shugui, the Prince of Ningjing, refused to live under the new order. His five concubines — a concubine being a wife of secondary rank in a great household — hanged themselves first, one after another, rather than be taken by the victors. He buried them here himself, gave his land away to farmers, and took his own life the next day. The temple was built in 1683 in front of the grave.

Read this as ancestor veneration rather than the worship of gods. There is no miracle story, no oracle to consult; these women are honoured because they were loyal, and loyalty is the virtue that Chinese tradition prizes above almost all others. Two servants who died with them have their own small shrine in the corner, the Yi Ling Jun tomb. The gravestones are plain, the courtyard is full of trees, and the whole place is deliberately undramatic.

Entry is free and it is usually open roughly 08:00 to 17:00 — verify at the gate, because it is locked outside those hours. This is a grave, so keep your voice down and skip the posed photos at the tomb itself. Then walk about a kilometre north up Nanmen Road, fifteen minutes, to the Confucius Temple, where the same dynasty tried to build a state out of books.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; it is a historic site and shrine, not a ticketed attraction. Verify the hours at the gate — the grounds are locked outside them.
stops.openingHours: Usually open daily, roughly 08:00 to 17:00. Confirm at the gate; the entrance is shut outside these hours.
stops.accessibility: A level courtyard and a low step or two into the shrine hall. Paths are paved, but the garden ground under the trees can be uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Find the small side shrine — the Yi Ling Jun tomb — for the two servants who died alongside the concubines; most visitors walk straight past it. And read the grave inscriptions before you raise a camera.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the temple garden, turn right, and walk north up Nanmen Road for about a kilometre, fifteen minutes. The Confucius Temple's boundary wall and its semicircular pond appear on your left, opposite Fuzhong Street. Go in through the main gate on Nanmen Road.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: eazytraveler, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tainan Confucius Temple
stops.narration:
You are standing at the first school in Taiwan. The complex in front of you went up in 1665, three years after the Dutch left, when Zheng Jing, Koxinga's son, took the advice of his chief minister Chen Yonghua and built a Confucian temple with an academy attached. After the Qing annexed the island in 1683 it became the prefectural academy for southern Taiwan, and it is still called the First Academy.

Confucius was not a god. He was a teacher and minor official who lived in China around 500 BCE, and what he taught was less salvation than conduct: respect your parents, keep your promises, study, govern fairly, perform the rituals properly. His followers turned those ethics into the examination system that ran China for a thousand years — a ladder of tests that could lift a farmer's son into the civil service. The temple reflects it. There are no painted door gods on the gates (the doors carry 108 metal studs instead), no couplets, and no idols of Confucius — only ancestral tablets in the main hall, because he is honoured rather than worshipped, and words were thought too small for him.

The grounds, the old lecture hall and the octagonal Wenchang Pavilion are free. The sanctuary beyond the Ta Cheng Gate — the main hall and its side wings — costs about NT$50, the New Taiwan dollar being the local currency. Hours are usually 08:30 to 17:30, closed on Lunar New Year's Eve; verify at the gate. Before you leave, find the stone stele near the entrance ordering all officials, soldiers and citizens to dismount from their horses. It was set up in 1687, in Chinese and Manchu script, and is the oldest surviving one in Taiwan. Then cross Nanmen Road into the old shopping lane.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The grounds, the lecture hall and the Wenchang Pavilion are free. The sanctuary beyond the Ta Cheng Gate — main hall and wings — is around NT$50. Prices change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Usually open daily, roughly 08:30 to 17:30, closed on Lunar New Year's Eve. Confirm at the gate.
stops.accessibility: The grounds are level and mostly step-free; the Ta Cheng Hall stands on a raised platform reached by a few steps, with a high wooden threshold at the door.
stops.insiderTip: Find the 1687 dismounting stele by the entrance — the oldest of its kind in Taiwan, carved in Chinese and Manchu. Then look at the Ta Cheng Gate doors: 108 studs and no painted gods, because Confucius is honoured, not served.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come out of the front gate and cross Nanmen Road at the lights, straight ahead. Fuzhong Street opens immediately in front of you under the stone arch — a minute's walk.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Fuzhong Street
stops.narration:
Step across the road and the mood changes. Fuzhong Street is a roughly two-hundred-metre lane of low shophouses whose front rooms open straight onto the pavement — drink stands, noodle counters, a sweet shop or two — and it begins under a stone arch that is the oldest thing in the lane.

That arch is the Pan Gong gateway of the old academy next door. In imperial China a pàn gōng was a school for the sons of princes, and only senior academies were allowed the semicircular pond and the gateway that went with the name. The arch marked the boundary between the school and the market, and the boundary is the point of this stop: Tainan's old streets are not museums, they are shops that never stopped trading. Look at how the buildings work — narrow frontage, deep interior, living quarters above the store, shutters that fold back into the wall, everything shaped for shade. On a January afternoon that design is still doing its job.

Now the same buildings sell bubble tea, handmade soap and coffee, and the city calls the mix wénchuàng, the "cultural and creative industry" — old shells, new businesses. Fuzhong has become one of the places where that experiment is most visible, so expect it to look both genuinely old and slightly self-aware. Eat something small while you are here: winter-melon tea, douhua (silken tofu pudding dressed with syrup), or a bowl of the sweet, savoury danzi noodles that Tainan claims as its own. Most businesses run from late morning into the early evening, and individual stands keep odd hours, so check as you go.

Then walk north-west up Fuzhong Street and Yongfu Road for about a kilometre, fourteen minutes, to a long red wall with five roof ridges rising behind it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Food, drinks and shops are at normal local prices; most stands still prefer cash, though some now take cards or mobile payment.
stops.openingHours: The street is open at all hours; most shops and food stands run roughly from late morning into the early evening. Individual hours vary — check as you go.
stops.accessibility: A flat, level lane with a smooth paved surface for most of its length; the stretch near the arch is narrower and slightly uneven. Crossings on Nanmen Road are not all kerb-ramped.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the Pan Gong arch at the entrance, then at the shophouse doors as you walk: narrow front, deep interior, shutters folding into the wall. People still live above the shops, so keep your voice down after dark.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back out of Fuzhong Street and head north-west up Yongfu Road for about a kilometre, fourteen minutes. The long red wall with the curved top and five rising roof ridges, on your right, is the God of War Temple.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Chainwit., CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: God of War Temple (Tainan Wu Temple)
stops.narration:
Here is a man who became a god. Guan Yu — Guan Gong, or Lord Guan — was a real general in the Three Kingdoms period of the third century CE, when China was split into three warring states. He was famous for loyalty: he stayed with his sworn lord through defeat and exile, refused to change sides, and was executed by an enemy around 220 CE. Emperors kept promoting the story, until he was worshipped as a god of war and loyalty — and, because he kept scrupulous accounts, as a patron of merchants and accountants.

The temple was built by Zheng Jing around 1663 to 1665, on ground tied to Koxinga and the Ming prince, and it was raised to official status in 1727, meaning the state itself performed sacrifices here. That rank shows in the architecture. Look for the low red wall along the road — locals call it the horseback wall, because it curves like a horse's bare back — and for the five different roof ridges rising behind it, the tallest in the swallowtail shape typical of Fujian, the province across the strait. At the door, count the iron studs: the central door has 72, the two side doors 54 each, every number a multiple of nine, which was reserved for royalty.

Inside there is more than one god, which is how Taiwanese temples actually work. Guan Gong stands at the main altar; a side hall holds Guanyin, the Buddhist figure of compassion; one small shrine is for Wenchang, who helps students pass exams; another is for Yue Lao, the matchmaker who ties couples together with a red thread. Entry is free and it is usually open 05:30 to 21:00 — verify at the gate. People come here to pray, so watch from the edges and never photograph anyone mid-prayer. Then step next door.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free; this is a working temple, not a ticketed site. Donations are welcome but never required. Verify the hours at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Usually open daily, roughly 05:30 to 21:00. Prayer times and festivals can change access — confirm at the gate.
stops.accessibility: A level courtyard, but every doorway has a raised wooden threshold to step over, and the passage behind the main altar is narrow when busy.
stops.insiderTip: Count the studs on the main door — 72 on the centre door, 54 on each side, all multiples of nine, the imperial number. The 'Da Zhang Fu' plaque above you, meaning 'man of character', was presented to the temple in 1791.
stops.nextStopDirections: Step out of the temple and walk about a hundred and fifty metres, two minutes, along Yongfu Road, then duck into the lane beside it. The Grand Mazu Temple's carved front hall is right there, sharing the same block.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 陳璿文, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Grand Mazu Temple
stops.narration:
Mazu is the goddess of the sea, and this is the first state-founded temple to her in Taiwan. Her story begins with a real woman: Lin Moniang, born on the Fujian coast around 960, who was said to walk on the waves to save drowning fishermen and died young. Sailors began praying to her, emperors kept enlarging her title, and by the Qing dynasty she was the Empress of Heaven — Tiānhòu in Mandarin. For an island of people who had crossed a dangerous strait to get here, she was the most practical deity going.

The building has a strange double life. It was finished in 1664, not as a temple but as the mansion of Zhu Shugui, the Prince of Ningjing — the same prince whose five concubines you met at the grave earlier on this walk. In 1683, after the Qing admiral Shi Lang took Taiwan from the Zheng family, he moved into the mansion and then had it converted into a temple to Mazu, partly to claim that the goddess had blessed the conquest. That political spin is why it is still called a 'sacrificial-rites' temple, guǎnsì: the state made the offerings.

Go into the main hall and look up. The gilded Mazu is enormous — about five and a half metres tall — carved, tradition says, by a Quanzhou craftsman more than three centuries ago, with two glaring guardians, Thousand-Mile Eyes and Favourable-Wind Ears, flanking her. Behind, the rear hall carries the human detail: the prince's old bedroom is now the Sacred Parents Hall, honouring Mazu's family and Prince Ningjing under one roof. Chinese folk religion keeps the dead close; here a goddess and a defeated prince share a house.

Entry is free, usually 06:00 to 21:00 — verify at the gate. Photograph the building freely; worshippers are not exhibits. Then walk a couple of minutes east to the fort the Dutch built.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry, as at most working temples in Tainan. Incense and offerings are optional; verify the current hours at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Usually open daily, roughly 06:00 to 21:00. Festivals — especially Mazu's birthday in the lunar third month — change the schedule. Confirm at the gate.
stops.accessibility: A level courtyard and halls, with a raised wooden threshold at each doorway and a couple of steps up to the main hall floor.
stops.insiderTip: Walk through to the rear hall: the prince's old bedroom is now the Sacred Parents Hall, honouring Mazu's family and Prince Ningjing together. It is the strangest and most human corner of the temple.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come out of the temple and turn right, then walk about two hundred metres, two minutes, east along Minzu Road. Chihkan Tower's red gateway and the white statue on the lawn are ahead on your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Felix Filnkoessl, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia)
stops.narration:
Under these Chinese pavilions is a European fort. In 1624 the Dutch East India Company — a Dutch trading firm with its own navy — built a base on the coast here, on a sandbar known as Tayouan, the name most scholars believe became 'Taiwan'. They wanted Chinese silk, porcelain and tea, Japanese silver, and this coast's deer skins and sugar, and a harbour junks could reach.

In 1653, to control the farming country inland, they raised Fort Provintia here, a few kilometres east of their main stronghold, Fort Zeelandia. It did not hold for long. In April 1661 a Ming loyalist warlord, Zheng Chenggong — known in the West as Koxinga, from a Hokkien phrase meaning roughly 'lord of the imperial surname' — landed with about twenty-five thousand men, took Provintia within days, and then besieged Zeelandia for nine months until the Dutch governor surrendered on 1 February 1662. Thirty-eight years of Dutch rule on Taiwan ended that day, and the island became the base for the Zheng family's hopeless campaign to win back the Ming throne from the Qing.

What you see now is a palimpsest — a surface written over. The original Dutch brickwork survives only in fragments; on and around the ruins the Qing, and later the Japanese, built the pavilions you are looking at, including the Sea God Temple and the Wenchang Pavilion, where students still come to pray to the god of examinations. On the lawn stands a statue of Koxinga receiving the Dutch surrender — a scene that never happened quite like that, and a reminder that monuments are arguments. The nine stone tortoises carrying inscribed slabs commemorate a 1780s rebellion against Qing rule, not the Dutch at all.

Entry is around NT$70 for adults, about NT$35 for students and seniors; it is usually open 08:30 to 21:30. Verify both at the gate. Then walk west to the old port lane.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around NT$70 for adults, roughly NT$35 for students, seniors, and some public employees. Prices change and only the on-site notice is final — verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Usually open daily, roughly 08:30 to 21:30, with the ticket office closing earlier. Verify at the gate.
stops.accessibility: A paved courtyard and level paths, but the pavilions are reached by stone steps and the upper floor by a steep stair. The site is not step-free beyond the ground level.
stops.insiderTip: The best thing here is out on the lawn: nine stone tortoises, each a bixi from dragon legend, carrying inscribed slabs the Qianlong emperor commissioned after a 1780s rebellion. Then find the old well said to have supplied the Dutch garrison.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the main gate and walk west along Minzu Road for about eight hundred metres, twelve minutes, into the old Five Channels district. Shennong Street is a narrow lane just north of Minquan Road, close to Haian Road — look for the Chinese arch over the entrance.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Shennong Street
stops.narration:
You are standing on a filled-in harbour. In the Qing dynasty this lane, then called Beishi Street, ran down to water: it was the entrance to the Five Channels, the canal-and-wharf district that kept Tainan trading after the great inner sea to the west, the Taijiang, silted up in the 1820s. Ships could no longer reach the old harbour, so merchants dug canals inland and moved goods through a grid of channels and godowns — warehouses stacked with rice, sugar and cloth. Shennong Street was the doorway to that world.

Read the buildings and you can still see the port. The ground floors sit low, near where a boat would tie up; the upper facades are narrow and tall, with carved wooden balconies and shuttered windows — living space above, commerce below. Look for the small shrines set into the houses, because merchants did not leave their gods at the shop door. Some of the old godowns and shophouses have been repaired, and the street now runs on two economies: at dusk the lanterns come on for photographers and the small bars and studios open, while by day it is mostly quiet and you can see the fabric of the place.

Tainan nearly lost this. After the canals were covered and the port moved away, the district decayed for much of the twentieth century, and its survival was partly an accident of poverty — for decades nobody had the money to knock it down and rebuild. Keep that pattern in mind across this city: what tourism now calls heritage, the last century called a slum. The street never closes and costs nothing, and some shops forbid photography inside, so read the signs and respect them. Then walk south to the food street.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Bars, cafés and studios along the lane charge their own prices; some shops ban photography inside, so ask or read the signs.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours. Shops and bars open mainly from the afternoon into the evening; mornings are quiet and best for looking at the buildings.
stops.accessibility: A narrow, flat lane with an uneven old stone-and-brick surface and a step at some doorways. It is not comfortable for wheelchairs during the busy evening hours.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the small house shrines and the carved wooden balconies above the shopfronts. At dusk the lanterns come on and the lane becomes the city's most photographed street — get there before the crowd does.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come out of Shennong Street on the town side and walk east for about eight hundred metres, eleven minutes, through the old port grid to Guohua Street. The food stands begin straight away, around the junction with Youai Street.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Andrzej Otrębski, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Guohua Street
stops.narration:
Guohua Street is not a night market and not a restaurant row; it is a working street where the same families have cooked at the same stands for generations. It runs along what was once a canal in the Five Channels district, on land that is entirely reclaimed — the whole south-west quarter of old Tainan sits on a silted lagoon, and that geology is the origin of the city's cooking. Rich river silt, a warm climate and easy irrigation made this the agricultural heartland of Taiwan: rice, sugar cane, and the shallow fish ponds that give the region its signature ingredient.

Learn three dishes while you are here. Beef soup, niúròu tāng, is breakfast food: thin slices of raw local beef dropped into boiling broth and served barely cooked, with a bowl of rice. Milkfish, shīmùyú in Mandarin, is the farmed fish of those coastal ponds — look for it as porridge or as belly soup, boneless and buttery. And danzi noodles, dànzǎi miàn, are a small bowl of thin noodles in a sweet prawn-and-pork broth, said to have been peddled by fishermen during their off-season. Tainan cooks sweeter than the rest of Taiwan — a little sugar in almost everything — and locals will tell you, without a flicker of doubt, that this is the best eating in the country. Taipei disagrees. Taipei is wrong.

Most stands trade from mid-morning into the evening, a few run later, and individual stalls close on odd days, so the street is busiest around lunch and again at dinner. Carry small notes. This is the end of the walk, and a worthy one: you have come from a prince's grave and a Dutch fort to the thing this city is genuinely famous for.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk; you pay only for what you eat. Bring small NT$ notes, since many stands still prefer cash, and check the price board.
stops.openingHours: Food stands usually trade from mid-morning into the evening, a few later still. Individual stalls vary and some close on odd days — check locally.
stops.accessibility: A level street with a mix of old pavement and raised thresholds at shop doors. It gets crowded, and motorbikes thread through the lanes, so stay alert.
stops.insiderTip: Order small portions from several stands instead of one big meal: a bowl of beef soup, then danzi noodles, then milkfish. Tainan food tastes sweet by the standards of the rest of Taiwan — taste before you reach for the seasoning.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Guohua Street is the all-day food street, best around lunch and at dinner; most stands close by mid-evening. If you are still out at night, the covered Xiaobei night market, a kilometre or so north-west, is a smaller and more local option with sit-down stalls — its opening nights have shifted over the years, so check before you commit. Otherwise, buses and taxis back to Tainan Station run from Minquan Road and the streets around it. Eat something before you go; you are, after all, in the best-fed city in Taiwan.
